title: Understanding the Individual
description: Distinguish emotional judgment, desire, time horizons and self-concept before interpreting outcomes.

lessons.title: What makes a judgment evidence-sensitive?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply irrationality while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: A preferred result may shape the evidence we seek. Contrast selective confirmation with testing a hypothesis against rival explanations.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A project manager deliberately asks an independent reviewer to find conditions under which a favored plan might fail.

lessons.title: Why does an object become desirable?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply covetousness while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Greene emphasizes imagined value and absence. Separate functional need, symbolic value and social proof; causal claims require comparisons.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A buyer checks actual product requirements before treating popularity as evidence of suitability.

lessons.title: How far ahead should a decision look?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply shortsightedness while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Immediate constraints matter, but delayed costs and uncertainty belong in the same assessment. Evaluate decisions using information available at the time.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A committee compares a quick launch with a staged trial and lists reversal costs.

lessons.title: Where does attitude end and circumstance begin?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply self-sabotage while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Expectations may influence interaction, yet outside constraints and mistreatment are real. A feedback loop is a hypothesis that needs observations.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A worker records specific barriers alongside their expectations instead of blaming every setback on mindset.

lessons.title: Can contradictory conduct reveal a hidden motive?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply repression while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Greene uses a shadow framework to interpret discrepancies. The discrepancy itself can be investigated without accepting a hidden motive as fact.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A leader claims to welcome feedback but repeatedly excludes critics; review the decisions, not a guessed personality.

lessons.title: How is ambition calibrated?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply grandiosity while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Confidence should remain open to feedback and uncertainty. A successful outcome does not establish exceptional predictive ability.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A founder writes a range of forecasts and tracks whether outcomes match them.

lessons.title: What turns purpose into action?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply aimlessness while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Purpose can organize decisions without implying a predetermined destiny. Concrete steps and revision keep goals grounded in circumstances.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A volunteer tests a chosen project in a small pilot before committing years to it.

lessons.title: What can mortality awareness teach?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply death denial while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Greene presents a reflective philosophical practice. Responses vary, and limited research does not validate a universal outcome.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A fictional reader reflects on priorities without demanding that others find meaning in loss.

title: Understanding Other People
description: Interpret social behavior with contextual evidence, empathy and meaningful alternatives.

lessons.title: How does self-focus affect empathy?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply narcissism while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Greene describes self-absorption and outward attention as competing orientations. Treat this as a literary framework, not a diagnostic scale.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A listener checks whether their summary of another person’s concern is accurate rather than assuming shared feelings.

lessons.title: What does presentation reveal?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply role-playing while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Social roles can change how people communicate without deception. Separate observable cues from explanations and inspect the relevant evidence limits.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A nervous presenter uses a steady voice while explaining a genuinely well-researched plan.

lessons.title: When does repetition become informative?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply compulsive behavior while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Repeated behavior is more informative when the surrounding conditions are comparable. A contextual pattern is not an invariant character judgment.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A team compares delays across projects with similar workloads and clear responsibilities.

lessons.title: What makes disagreement legitimate?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply defensiveness while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Self-image and autonomy can affect resistance, but an objection may also be correct. Respect meaningful choice and assess the substance.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A manager asks what would make a proposed change acceptable without penalizing disagreement.

lessons.title: When is comparison harmful?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply envy while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Social comparison may involve admiration, disappointment or envy. Behavior and procedural evidence matter more than imagined inner motives.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: An award committee reviews fairness complaints against published rules.

lessons.title: How do roles constrain behavior?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply gender rigidity while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Greene’s gender framework is an authorial interpretation. Examine social expectations and individual variation without treating stereotypes as innate laws.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A hiring panel applies the same behavioral criteria to every candidate.

lessons.title: What separates assertiveness from aggression?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply aggression while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Firm boundaries can be ethical; threats or coercive conduct warrant attention. Evaluate behavior and impact without guessing motive.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: Two teams negotiate a deadline and document agreed responsibilities rather than escalating personal accusations.

title: Understanding Groups, Power and Society
description: Separate group influence, accountable leadership and historical context from individual motives.

lessons.title: How does a group reach agreement?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply conformity while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Public consensus can reflect evidence, pressure, or both. Seek independent reasons and conditions that allow dissent.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A committee collects private views before and after a new report.

lessons.title: What makes authority credible?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply fickleness while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Leadership can draw on competence, accountability and institutional roles. Popularity and obedience do not uniquely identify legitimacy.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A supervisor invites objections and documents revisions to a plan.

lessons.title: How can historical context be assessed?
lessons.objective: Explain and apply generational myopia while distinguishing evidence from inference.
lessons.introduction: Age, period and cohort are intertwined. Historical narratives can inspire hypotheses but do not establish uniform generational traits.
lessons.illustration: Fictional example: A researcher compares repeated surveys rather than attributing one age difference to birth year.
